name: Scutellaria baicalensis root extract
lead: Scutellaria baicalensis root extract comes from Baikal skullcap, also called Chinese skullcap, a mint-family plant whose dried root (huangqin) is one of the 50 fundamental herbs of traditional Chinese medicine [1]. Its main flavonoids include baicalin, baicalein and wogonin [1]. In cosmetics it is used as an anti-inflammatory, antioxidant or brightening botanical, in creams and serums aimed at calmer, more even-toned skin.

People use products containing it for the look of the skin: the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant character attributed to its flavonoids is the basis for its inclusion in products for redness-prone skin and for hyperpigmentation or dull tone. The root is recorded in the Chinese, European and British pharmacopoeias [2].

Laboratory studies report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, and a 2025 safety assessment reviewed its use as a cosmetic ingredient [3][4][5]. A case report documents allergic contact dermatitis to a cosmetic containing it [6]. Two small registered trials have tested creams for hyperpigmentation, though results were not located [7][8].

paras: Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi is a flowering plant of the Lamiaceae family, native to China, Korea, Mongolia and the Russian Far East and Siberia [1]. In traditional Chinese medicine, huangqin usually refers to the dried root, and the term also covers roots of related species [1]. A 2018 review reports that 126 small molecules and 6 polysaccharides have been isolated from the plant, in classes including free flavonoids, flavonoid glycosides and phenylethanoid glycosides [2]. The classical formula Huangqin-Tang has been used in China for thousands of years and has been reviewed for ulcerative colitis [9].
The name skullcap is applied to over 200 plants, so the scientific name is preferred, and North American skullcap (S. lateriflora) is sometimes confused with S. baicalensis [1].

Baicalin, baicalein and wogonin are the flavonoids most often discussed; baicalein is the aglycone of baicalin, which is a glycoside [10]. Traditional uses described in reviews include antibacterial and antiviral applications, and the classical decoction Huangqin-Tang has been studied for ulcerative colitis [9][10].

Baicalein, the aglycone of baicalin, is described in reviews as a potent free radical scavenger and xanthine oxidase inhibitor, and baicalin as an anti-inflammatory agent [10]. In vitro studies report that a wogonin-rich fraction suppressed IL-1beta-induced inflammatory signalling in human osteoarthritic chondrocytes, and that root extracts protected lipid membranes from peroxidation in rat lung mitochondria [3][4]. A review of baicalin describes effects mediated by oxidative stress and inflammation pathways in liver and gut disease models [11], and wogonin has been studied extensively in preclinical cancer research [12]. These are non-skin models and non-cosmetic endpoints.

Huangqin appears in traditional Chinese herbal medicine and in modern supplements and cosmetic formulations alike [1][2]. In cosmetics, the Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety lists functions of the plant-derived ingredients as antimicrobial, skin conditioning, antioxidant, skin protectant and fragrance, among others [5]. Within appearance communities it appears as one ingredient in botanical skincare rather than as a standalone topic of discussion.

The International Journal of Toxicology published the Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety assessment of four S. baicalensis-derived ingredients in 2025. The panel concluded that S. baicalensis root extract and root powder are safe in cosmetics under the present practices of use and concentration described, and that the available data were insufficient to determine safety for the plain extract and sprout extract under reported conditions of use [5]. A case report described allergic contact dermatitis to a cosmetic containing resveratrol and S. baicalensis root extract [6]. Wikipedia, citing the LiverTox database, notes case reports and small case series of acute liver injury with jaundice that began one to three months after starting herbal or dietary supplements containing the plant [1]. A review of herb-drug interactions covers herbal products in general [13].

Human data on skin outcomes are limited to registered trials and a case report. No published results from controlled trials of S. baicalensis creams for hyperpigmentation were located; the case report of allergic contact dermatitis is the main published human skin report [6].

Two registered trials examined creams containing the extract for hyperpigmentation: a 2025 study of a huangqin cream (n=38) and a 2023 study of a topical cream for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in Malaysians (n=25) [7][8]. Published outcomes are not available. In other conditions, a randomized trial of 58 ankylosing spondylitis patients compared a huangqin-containing capsule with salazosulfapyridine, and a phase I trial studied baicalein tablets in healthy Chinese subjects [14][15].

card.summary: Chinese skullcap root extract used as an anti-inflammatory or brightening ingredient, with small trials registered but little published human evidence.
card.note: Contact allergy reported; oral products linked to liver injury case reports.

quick.overview:
A root extract from Baikal skullcap, a staple of traditional Chinese medicine, now used in some skincare for anti-inflammatory or brightening claims.

Evidence is mostly lab studies; two small hyperpigmentation cream trials are registered.
quick.mechanism: Flavonoids such as baicalin and wogonin showed antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in cell and animal studies.
quick.risks: A case report describes contact allergy to a cosmetic containing it, and oral supplements have been linked to liver injury in case reports.

angle.text: Skincare brands include the extract for soothing and brightening claims, and small trials of huangqin creams for hyperpigmentation are registered. People use it in leave-on products aimed at redness and uneven tone.
